speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on his speech which I believe contained some insight. However, he talked about a martial plan. Instead of sending in the marshall, the problem is that this Government has sent in the sheriff. The sheriff has said: "We are taking back and repossessing everything you have".
Just to put into perspective the resolution which is before us today, let me say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Question Period painted a glowing picture of what is happening with respect to job-creation in Canada. He quoted this from The Globe and Mail: "Creation of 304,000 jobs drives unemployment down". If the Prime Minister had read on to the last four paragraphs, I think he would have put into perspective the resolution we have before us today. As a graphic example of what we are talking about, The Globe and Mail stated:
Still, the silver lining has a cloud. The job creation machine appears to have ignored residents of Canada's hinterlands. Raw figures show that between November, 1984, and last month, most of the new jobs were packed into the country's heartland, while the demand for new workers petered out going either west or east.
If the growth in jobs had been evenly spread across the country, each province would have one share of the new jobs roughly equal to its share of the labour force.
In the past year, Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick were the biggest winners.
All got more than their share of the new employment. Together they have almost two-thirds of the labour force, but picked up almost 84 per cent of the new jobs in the past year.
Here is the message I want to get across, Mr. Speaker:
The outermost provinces-British Columbia, Alberta, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia-did worst. With 26 per cent of the work force ... they got only 8 per cent of the new jobs.
When the Government talks about the rosy picture across the country in job creation, we have to put it in perspective and illustrate the figures which point out why we have this resolution before the House today.
The people of the Atlantic provinces have always struggled to stay afloat. However, since this Government took power there seems to have been a consistent policy of taking away whatever life preservers we have had. The problem is that there is an ideological inflexibility over there. There is a flaw in the policy which says that somehow the private sector is going to solve all our ills. For the first time in 30 years in this country there is no regional development policy. My colleague from Cape Breton said it was our Party which created the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. That was a victory for regional development. However, there is now in Canada no policy for regional development and that is why the Atlantic provinces are suffering. You cannot inflexibly apply one policy all across Canada. Canada is a collection of regions and the Atlantic provinces have always depended on public sector support to shore up the weak private sector. There is
nothing wrong with putting the private sector front and centre, but in the Atlantic provinces the private sector is weak and there has to be Government involvement. In the past there has been Government involvement but it is absent now. In the meantime, the Government programs we have depended on have been cut back.
Let me start with the Established Programs Financing, transfer payments, because therein lies the greatest tragedy of all. There will be less money going to the Atlantic provinces, including my own, than had been anticipated, hoped for and expected. As a result there will be increased charges for hospitals and post-secondary institutions. Young people, the real hope for Atlantic Canada, will have a tough time getting the education and training they need. In the long run the most tragic cut of all will be that cut in the Established Programs Financing.
I want to look at the cuts in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Something like $25 million will be cut from that Department which is so important to my province. There will be lay-offs in the Department, about 170 people across Canada. Some provinces depend more heavily on the fishery and it is logical to assume that we will probably lose more of those civil servants in the Atlantic than elsewhere in Canada. Therefore, the cuts in the area of small-craft harbours and lay-offs in the Civil Service will add to an already disastrous situation. As well, the issue of factory-freezer trawlers emphasizes again the insensitivity of this Government to what is needed in Atlantic Canada. If this approach to factory-freezer trawlers is allowed to be developed, if more licences are issued, it will have a devastating effect on the northeast coast of Newfoundland which is in my riding. If factory-freezer trawlers are allowed to multiply, the whole inshore fishery along the northeast coast will be devastated, indeed wiped out. The only alternative for these people will be what my colleague from Cape Breton mentioned this morning, an exodus from the Atlantic provinces to elsewhere in Canada. That none of us can tolerate. There are no plans to help the people on the northeast coast who will be dislocated because of these trawlers. There are no programs for retraining, for developing alternatives in the inshore fishery. No examination, no plan, and that is where the Government stands condemned on this whole issue.
The Government has not only not responded to the longterm problems in the fishery, it has not responded adequately to emergencies. In October I raised in the House with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) the disastrous situation in the inshore fishery. There was no crop there this year. The fish did not come inshore. Many people along the northeast coast and in other parts of Newfoundland and Labrador will not qualify for unemployment insurance. In October I told the Minister not to wait until the end of the fishing season, but institute work programs now and give these people a chance to have an income this winter. The Minister waited until the fishing season was over and responded with too little, too late. We received $9.5 million which I estimate is half or less than half of what is needed to do the job


in job creation in the Newfoudland fishery. The Government was told about this but it did not react to a real emergency and for that it stands condemned as well.
In addition, the regular job-creation program is not working. This year the Minister built a training component into what is the successor to the Canada Works program. If you are going to apply for a job-creation project now in Newfoundland or the Atlantic provinces, you have to show you can train people for long-term jobs. It is naive and nonsensical to apply a policy like that to the Atlantic area. There is no way that kind of training program can be built in. The Government and the Minister have to realize that. She has to change the policy, and reinstitute Canada Works if workers in the Atlantic provinces are going to get jobs and have the income they need over the winter. This job development program has to be changed, this training component has to be wiped out, and we have to get back to the job-creation programs we had previously. As well, the situation in youth job creation is bad. I want to read some figures from the Minister's own Department which show that under Challenge '85, Newfoundland young people earned less money per hour, worked for a shorter period of time, and earned less over-all than young people anywhere else in Canada. Young Newfoundlanders earned an average of $1,232 compared with a national average of $2,000. Newfoundlanders earned an average of $4.09 per hour compared with a national average of $4.73. If we add that to the figures I read from The Globe and Mail earlier we can see that there may be an advance in other parts of Canada but it has not happened in Atlantic Canada. Indeed, that area of the country is slipping farther behind. In the meantime, no action has been taken to shore up the economy with public sector support which we so badly need. As a matter of fact, programs which had been announced have been cancelled. For example, a federal prison announced for central Newfoundland has not gone ahead. It was announced one year ago last fall and this is December, 1985. We still have no word on that project. This is the kind of public sector support we need to create jobs in the Atlantic area and that is the kind of project this Government, with its private sector ideology, has cancelled.
The only thing that the present Government is hanging its hat on in Newfoundland, as far as I can see, is the Atlantic Accord. Given the situation now with OPEC and the prospects for world oil prices, the development of Hibernia, as much as I want it to go ahead, is questionable. It is certainly questionable if we see it as the total economic saviour of Newfoundland. Newfoundland may get $200 million a year from the Hibernia project, but the deficit of Newfoundland is something like $300 million a year. If the present Government is hanging its economic hat on the Hibernia development, it will be sadly mistaken. We need the kind of public sector input which my Party put into my province when it was the Government of Canada. It instituted a water system in Port aux Basques at a cost of $6 million, a music school at Memorial at a cost of $2 million, a world-class marine institute at a cost of $47 million, and an ocean industries agreement to help small business get a leg up in going after jobs in the offshore.
Supply
The Liberal Government instituted a tourism agreement at a cost of $14 million to help small business to respond to the increased traffic in the Atlantic area, and a minerals agreement which prompted exploration which resulted in finds such as the gold deposit on the south coast of Newfoundland. That minerals agreement was made at a cost of $21 million. The Liberal Government made the Burin Peninsula agreement at a cost of $28 million which has resulted in the start-up of projects such as the mine at St. Lawrence. There was a rural development agreement which funds incentives by volunteers all over the province. That involved a cost of $18 million. There was also a roads agreement.
Those are the kind of projects, programs, and policies that the Liberal Party had when it was the Government of Canada and that is the kind of public sector support which is absent now. The Government has even cancelled a very important project, the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation. I asked the previous Minister of Fisheries and Oceans about that and he confirmed that the $15 million which had been set aside to create the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation has evaporated. It no longer exists. The Government has been in power for over a year and we still do not have the vehicle which is so important to northern Newfoundland and Labrador.
Fisheries Products International has just said that it will be getting rid of 23 plants. Many of those plants are in small communities which are very vulnerable indeed. Without support, help, confidence, and money from the Government, there is no way that those plants in those communities can survive. They need the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation which the present Liberal Party proposed but which the Government has not seen fit to proceed with. Indeed, it has seen fit to spend that money elsewhere.
In my estimation, Mr. Speaker, the north is probably the hardest hit of all. The people in the north are usually the forgotten people of Canada. I speak not only of the people in Labrador, but those in Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories as well. The deregulation of transportation will mean increased costs for people in the north because they depend so heavily on air transportation.
I would like to point out one particular issue in the north which I believe needs immediate attention by the Government, that is the isssue of taxation of northern benefits. In his economic statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that he would continue the moratorium, that is the nontaxation of northern benefits such as housing and travel until the end of 1985. We are getting very close to the end of 1985 and there has been no statement from the Government as to what it intends to do about the taxation of northern benefits.
This is not a national issue in the country, but the people who live in Whitehorse, Yellowknife, Old Crow, Labrador City and Goose Bay, as well as some people in northern New Brunswick and northern British Columbia are very, very concerned about this particular issue. It particularly affects mining communities such as Farrow in the Yukon. There are


Adjournment Motion
special benefits for people who live and work in the north and the Government must say very clearly that in the future, as in the past, those benefits will not be taxed because, if that happens, it will put an increased economic burden on people at a time when they can least afford to bear it. The Government must measure up to its responsibilities in the north. It is one thing to let the Polar Sea go through the Northwest Passage, but it is another thing altogether to take money out of the pockets of people who live in that area.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in defence of the motion before the House today, I have tried to say that the record of the Government in the Atlantic provinces is, indeed, utterly dismal. The people know it. That is why the polls show that, although there are only four points separating the two Parties nationally, there is a ten-point spread in favour of my Party in the Atlantic Provinces. That seems to me to be as dramatic an indication as any that I can use of the knowledge of the people that the present policies are not going to work and that the Government has failed to live up to its responsibilities. I find it amazing that a Government with such an overwhelming mandate to govern should dissipate that right to govern so quickly.
What the Government is doing to the economy of the Atlantic area is even more serious. If the present Government policies of user-pay, deregulation, cuts in government services and private sector front and centre at all costs are not changed, corrected and reversed, the Atlantic provinces will slide silently into the Atlantic Ocean. If the Government continues on that course, it will see that happen. At the very least, it is ignoring the Atlantic economy, and at the worst, it is goring the economy of the Atlantic area.

speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 46, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis)- Health-Breast implants-Request for stricter control and additional research funds; the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong)-Airports-Automobile rental policy, (b) Request for committee hearing; the Hon. Member for Broad-view-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald)-Trade-Canada-United States negotiations-Prime Minister's speech in Chicago, (b) Magazine publishing industry.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Dingwall:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of the people of Atlantic Canada in its demonstrated lack of political will to provide jobs and other economic opportunities to the people of that region.

I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to some of the comments made by the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). He suggested that the record of the Government is dismal in the Atlantic area. He did mention the Atlantic Accord, but suggested that the Government is hanging its head on that particular measure with little to back it up. I do not think that is the case at all. I think the Government can hold its head high over the Atlantic Accord which is an outstanding agreement when you consider the benefits that will flow to Newfoundland in particular and to the Atlantic area as a whole.
I will mention a few of the other benefits which the Members from Newfoundland may like to be reminded of. Just a few days ago the Minister responsible for CMHC entered into an agreement whereby a new $700,000 senior citizen housing unit will be built in Mount Pearl in conjunction with the Legion in that community. There was a recent announcement on the launching of a new ferry vessel, Caribou, at a cost to the federal Government of approximately $121 million. The Government of Canada made an investment in the equity capital of Fishery Products International to put the company on a sound footing for the future. That was an investment made in the last eight weeks of some $76.7 million. There was an official ceremony celebrating the completion of the highway connecting Conception Bay south to the Trans-Canada highway, which project cost a total of $12.8 million. The federal contribution for that was some $9.6 million. Just recently there was the official opening of the Newfoundland-Labrador Institute of Fisheries and Marine Technology.
Liberal policy.

That was a total cost of $42 million, $29.7 million of which was from the federal treasury. On November 1, there was the official opening of the new music school building at Memorial University. The total cost was $5 million with a contribution from the Government of Canada of some $2 million.
On November 5, there was the official opening of the National Research Council Institute for Marine Dynamics, including the world's largest Arctic vessel research facility and ice tank. The cost to the Government of Canada was $55 million for that one project alone. On November 18 there was the official opening of the Marine Emergency Duty Centre. This is another program costing some $4.2 million.


In that list from the last eight weeks there is nearly $300 million worth of federal contributions to Newfoundland and Labrador. I think that is a remarkable and significant record.
Let us look at some programs for fishermen and fish plant workers because all of us know that it has been a difficult season for Newfoundland fishermen. In June, the Government instituted a special program for inshore fishermen who were prevented from commencing the inshore season by unusual ice conditions. That program was instituted to give such fishermen payments equivalent to the payments they would have received under the UI program if it was applicable. As a result, some 5,854 fishermen were assisted at a cost of $4.7 million.
I could go on at some length. I am sure Members opposite would want to be reminded of the commitment which the Government of Canada has continued to make to the Province of Newfoundland.
Previous Government.
Of course, these are events which have taken place within the last eight weeks.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member has a duty to respond on behalf of his Party. However, being the Hon. Member that he is, I also know that he would not want to mislead the House. He is in very great danger of doing that.
I happen to know whereof I speak because I served as the Newfoundland Minister in the previous administration. The reality is that every project he has mentioned, with the exception of the injection into Fisheries Products International, was implemented under the previous Liberal administration. The Caribou project began under our administration. I happened to sign the Conception Bay highway agreement myself. That is a matter of record. The Marine Institute, costing $47 million, was money that was commissioned by us and indeed the construction started when we were the Government of Canada. I was at the opening two weeks ago.
The music school was another project that started when we were the Government of Canada. The National Research Council goes back beyond my time to the time of Don Jamieson. The Marine Emergency Centre was instituted by Jean-Luc Pepin when he was Minister of Transport. All of those projects began under a Liberal administration and that was exactly the point I was making. We are public sector conscious whereas the Government is private sector conscious.
It is important to emphasize that the only thing the Hon. Member mentioned that his Government did was to inject $105 million into Fisheries Products International. It is also important to note that as a result of that, it has drained every single cent of economic development money for all of Newfoundland for this year. There will not be another project. It is important that all those people from Newfoundland who are watching and all those in the Chamber realize that the $105 million comes from an economic development envelope that is put aside every year for every province. As a result of that injection into Fisheries Products International there is no more
Supply
money for economic development projects in the Province of Newfoundland.
If I am wrong, I would like someone opposite to correct me, but I believe that the fact is that that $105 million injected into Fisheries Products International is not new money but money from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion under the economic development envelope for economic projects in Newfoundland. This means that there will be no new initiatives such as the ones we have taken in the past. That is the reality and the truth.

Would the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) comment on the opinion of Mr. Peckford, the Premier of Newfoundland, and give us his opinion on the total effect of the issuance of the factory-freezer trawler licences? How will it affect plant workers in Newfoundland and indeed the inshore fishery of Newfoundland? Does he see that as being a long-term threat to the inshore fishery?
There are those who believe that the capital cost of bringing in factory-freezer trawlers may well put extra pressure on the fishing industry and indeed allow for further quotas for factory-freezer trawlers in order to make them economically feasible in the long term to te detriment of the inshore fishery?

There is no question that it will be an either/or situation. You cannot catch fish twice and you cannot process fish twice. If they are caught offshore, they cannot be caught inshore and if they are processed offshore they will not be processed inshore. There is no question that there is a threat to jobs in inshore plants.
My greatest concern in this whole debate about factory-freezer trawlers is that there has been no enunciation of any long-term plan for the inshore fishery of Newfoundland, for the people in the plants and the fishermen. No one has given any thought to that.
Those are the people who are in jeopardy and they are among the most disadvantaged and vulnerable groups anywhere in Canada. The real tragedy today is that no one in Government is giving thought to what will happen to the inshore fishery, particularly along the northeast coast of Newfoundland. I have not heard one word in this whole debate on factory-freezer trawlers addressing that situation.
There is no question that it is a threat and the Government must live up to its responsibility and make clear its intention for the inshore fishery, particularly for the northeast coast of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the Member for a very articulate and succinct speech, especially in light of the rebuttal wiht the ridiculous claims made by Members opposite. They are so desperate to find something good to say that they had to go back to the Liberal record to find some positive announcements to recant.
I know that the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador has made the same inquiries as I have. Has he received any assurance from the Government of Canada,


Supply
despite repeated requests by us and the people living in the area, about the future of the northern fisheries development corporation? This project was conceived under the last administration, during the time he was in Cabinet, but we have heard nothing about it ever since.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) points out an issue that is important to him and myself as well as the people we serve together. As I said in my speech, if nothing is done 23 plants will be cut adrift by Fisheries Products International. Fisheries Products International says that it will be getting rid of these plants because they are non-productive.
If no plan is put in place, those small communities in his riding and mine will not only be vulnerable, their whole economic base is in danger of being destroyed.
We have proposed a public sector corporation, a northern fisheries development corporation. Not only has the Government not put this in place, it has taken the $15 million which we had put aside to fund that corporation and used it elsewhere. That cannot be excused and must be condemned.
My hon. friend and I must continue to fight to establish that northern fisheries development corporation for plants on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and along the coast of Labrador. Only with that kind of support will those people who are very disadvantaged and vulnerable be able to survive.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even after what we have just heard, it should not come as a surprise that I welcome this opportunity to inform the House that the Government has not abandoned the Atlantic provinces, as claimed by the Opposition.
The Conservative Government has now been in office for fifteen months, and I think Canadians know what we have done and the results we have achieved.
Before elaborating on the situation in the Atlantic provinces, Mr. Speaker, I would like to give a general overview of the national situation, which in itself constitutes a very encouraging indicator of our economy.
I would remind the House that unemployment has dropped
I.	5 per cent since we came to power. This is remarkable progress indeed, at a time when our economic recovery is still somewhat shaky.
During the first quarter of 1985, the GNP growth rate increased 33 per cent compared with the first quarter in 1984. During the same period, interest rates fell, dropping from
II.	25 per cent at the end of 1984 to their present level which is around 10 per cent. In August 1985, retail sales increased by
12.6 per cent over the previous year, and things are continuing to improve.
These figures are enough to make the Opposition blush with embarrassment, since they are supported by the projections of the Economic Council of Canada, which is announcing ten years of steady growth, moderate inflation and a progressive decline in the unemployment rate.
The ECC is predicting an average annual growth of 3.5 per cent during the next ten years, a rate of inflation of less than 4 per cent and a drop in the unemployment rate which should stabilize at around 7.6 per cent between now and 1991.
And now I would like to get back to what has been done to help the Atlantic provinces. The Government of Canada has signed an agreement with Prince Edward Island on electric power rates. This step involves funding of over $50 million and is aimed at bringing down existing power rates in this province. One of the aspects of this agreement is a provisional, shared-cost subsidiary agreement, with a budget of $8.5 million, of which $6.8 million is being provided by the federal Government, Furthermore, a special advisor has been appointed to explore all possible avenues regarding a long term solution to the Island's energy problems.
This Government has signed agreements on tourism and market development, within the framework of the general agreements. It has also provided $4.5 million to establish a new meat processing plant to replace the Canada Packers plant.
The Government has provided this province with funding totalling $103 million under the Economic Regional Development Agreement.
As for Newfoundland, last spring, the federal and provincial governments signed a joint agreement under which $180 million will be set aside for improvements to Newfoundland's road network. Under the ERDA, $150 million will be injected into upgrading the Trans-Canada Highway and $30 million will be allocated for roads in Labrador. The federal contribution amounts to $112.5 million; in addition, $93 million have been allocated to the Goose Bay airport development project, and a $6.5 million contribution has been used to improve the quality of Channel-Port-aux-Basques municipal drinking water.
All told, under the regional economic development agreement, the federal Government will have invested over $235 million in Newfoundland over a five-year period.
Members of the Opposition also referred to Nova Scotia. In May 1985, eight new members were appointed to the Cape Breton advisory committee to consider ways in which the federal and provincial Governments might promote employment and long-term economic development in Cape Breton.
The Canadian Government has also approved the final project for the construction of a second access tunnel to the Donken-Morien underwater coal deposits at Cape Breton.


Drilling for this 3.5-kilometre tunnel will take a year, at an estimated cost of $16 million. Capital expenditures fall within Devco's current budgetary appropriations and, in line with our terms of reference, the tunnel drilling project attests to the federal Government's commitment towards Cape Breton. It will boost the local economy and create 100 jobs in the Glace Bay region.
Under the regional industrial development program, the Government gave Nova Scotia Pulp Limited about $4 million to upgrade its pulp and paper plant, make its operations more profitable, and thus contribute to maintaining jobs in the region of Port Hawkesbury.
Again in May 1985, DRIE gave a $1.5 million grant to Glace Bay's Highland Fisheries for the construction of a modern fish processing plant valued at $6.3 million. Thanks to that assistance, the plant will have 180 employees before the end of 1985.
In July 1985 the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) announced Government support payments to complete the federal assistance program made available to Cape Breton under the regional industrial development program and other DRIE projects. These support payments and the Cape Breton investment tax credit which then increased 50 to 60 per cent have turned this region into a haven for investors.
Both Governments agreed last June to act jointly to bring forward various economic development projects under the Canada-Nova-Scotia Economic Regional Development Agreement.
The new action plan proposes cooperative efforts under the two subsidiary agreements on technological transportation and innovation. The signatory Ministers took this opportunity to change the priorities of the ERDA to reflect their views about the importance of consultations with the native people and the visible minorities of the province about ERDA issues which concern them. Indeed, we saw at the recent First Ministers' Conference that these are priority issues for the province. The subsidiary agreements already signed under the ERDA have a total value of $205.5 million, of which the Federal share will be $140 million.
The Cape Breton Advisory Committee created by the two Governments and chaired by Mrs. Theresa MacNeil is a perfect example of federal-provincial cooperation. Last September, the committee submitted a report based on its consultations with Cape Breton residents last summer. The recommendations contained in this report have been carefully evaluated and have already influenced the decisions of the Federal Government. For instance, the boundaries for the Cape Breton tax credit have been extended to the Mulgrave Region in the Southwest, and the benefits of the tax credit have been increased.
Last Friday, on December 6, a new agency called Enterprise Cape Breton was created. Its purpose is to stimulate economic
Supply
development in the region. While this is a federal initiative, the participation of the private sector and the province will be welcome and even essential. Based on the one counter formula. Enterprise Cape Breton will enable eventual investors to be better informed about DREE programs and services, and will operate with a $25 million budget, which is double the budget of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Enterprise Canada will also launch major promotion and marketing programs to attract investments to Canada.
If we look at all these projects, we can see that our federal projects have already begun to create jobs in Cape Breton, as indicated by the announcement of $10 million worth of industrial development and expansion projects.
Last June, Magma International Inc. signed a memorandum of agreement with the Federal Government to locate in Cape Breton. Magma is a company which has been very successful in operating small semi-independent facilities, for instance in Southwestern Ontario. It is considering the construction on Cape Breton Island of a center similar to the one it already operates in Ontario for training in state-of-the art technology.
Again in Nova Scotia, over $1 million have been allocated for repairing the Port Hawkesbury road, and $200,000 for developing an industrial area in Antigonish. Those amounts have been expended under the Canada-Nova Scotia supplementary agreement on the Strait of Canso.
And to promote access to modern technology, a $34 million economic and regional development agreement was signed with Nova Scotia in July 1985 to set up computer and high technology training centers. Ottawa will assume 70 per cent of the cost, with the Province contributing the other 30 per cent.
Again under ERDA, the Federal Government has therefore injected another $140 million in Nova Scotia.
Let me turn now to New Brunswick. A $32 million supplementary agreement was signed in November 1984 relating to tourism, with a $22 million federal contribution. And, yesterday, on December 9, $30 million were allotted for industrial development in that Province, with the signing in Fredericton of an industrial development supplementary agreement. The federal Government will provide $21 million through M1RD, and the Province $9 million.
Under another agreement signed in May 1985 under 1RDP, the Canadian Government will contribute $42 million, $10 million of which are refundable, for the setting up in Newcastle of a coated paper mill. The Acadia Paper Company is being financed by Repap Enterprise Incorporated from Montreal.
That project will provide employment stability to more than 1,600 forest and mill workers, and involves the hiring of 1,000 person-years during the construction phase. An estimated 125 permanent jobs will thus be created.
The Canadian Government has provided that Province with $215.7 million under ERDA.

Mr. Speaker, from January 1984 to March 1985, 3,100 loans totalling $98 million were guaranteed under the Small Business Loans Act in Atlantic Canada. Under the Industrial Regional Development Program, we have been able to contribute a total of $90 million for 209 projects.
Mr. Speaker, more than any other Government, this Government has promoted an exchange of views and improved relations between the federal Government and the provinces. For the first time in the history of this country, the Chairman of the Cabinet Committee responsible for Regional Economic Development, the Hon. Sinclair Stevens, scheduled regular meetings with his provincial counterparts. Since the first meeting in Ottawa in January 1985, meetings have been held every two months in provincial capitals across the country to discuss the difficult problems of regional development. These meetings provide an opportunity for discussing economic development and for setting up a development policy adapted to the needs of the various regions of this country. These meetings provide a forum for discussing questions such as co-ordinating assistance to small businesses through partial decentralization of the Industrial and Regional Development Program, reducing the number of regulations and the paper burden for small businesses, co-ordinating investment promotion activities and consulting on federal proposals for revising regulations for the transportation industry.
The Ministers responsible for regional economic development have agreed on a workplan for dealing with three broad objectives connected with regional development, namely, attracting and especially maintaining investment in all regions, enumerating obstacles to interprovincial trade as well as the various ways in which it could be enhanced, and preparing a data base on regional development. Two federal-provincial task forces have been created to examine these issues, and their reports will be submitted for consideration by the Ministers at their next meeting in January 1986.
Mr. Speaker, we have never seen the like of the economic potential that exists in the world today. Canada must take advantage of these opportunities and carve out its share of the market.
In concluding, 1 still wonder why Opposition Members are not prepared to invest their energies and work together with the Government to ensure that programs and initiatives produce results as quickly as possible, for the greater benefit of all Canadians.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. The Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson).

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. Concerning the situation in Cape Breton, obviously her speech was written before the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) answered a question in the House today. Quite clearly
he stated that very little happened to improve the economy of Cape Breton, or indeed Atlantic Canada, in the last year and a half. It is in that context that I mention her Department obviously wrote her speech yesterday. That she had to rise and read that speech is not good enough for Atlantic Canada. The people of Atlantic Canada are looking for some action from the Government. They are not looking for words. Actions speak louder than words.
On the very important issue of transfer payments to the provinces, I have in my possession a clipping from The Evening Times Globe of Saint John headed "Baxter Blasts Federal Cuts". Mr. John B. M. Baxter, Q.C., the Minister of Finance for the Province of New Brunswick, is reported as follows:
New Brunswick's health and education programs are "at serious risk" under an inflexible plan for slashing $2 billion from transfer payments to provinces advanced by federal Finance Minister Michael Wilson on Wednesday-
Depending on what method Wilson ultimately employs, Baxter says New Brunswick could lose either $60 million or $120 million in health and education transfer payments.
Those are the comments of the Minister of Finance for the Province of New Brunswick. We have heard other Ministers and Premiers from Atlantic Canada state clearly that cuts in transfer payments will affect Atlantic Canada. In fact, they will affect most provinces, but certainly Atlantic Canada.
How can the Hon. Member rise in her place today and say that what the Government has done in the last year and a half is beneficial to Atlantic Canada? How can she justify that? Also I would like her to justify how job-creation programs, such as the new Canadian Jobs Strategy invoked by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), will help my province and the Province of Newfoundland, which is in such bad shape that it will take 10 years of good Liberal administration for it to experience decent economic times?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What a dreamer!
How can the Hon. Member say that the new Canadian Jobs Strategy of the Government will be beneficial to my Province of Prince Edward Island when unemployment is the highest it has been since 1980?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that the question of my colleague makes me smile. When he talks about a Liberal administration whose benefits we are reaping today, I think he is right. The problem we are experiencing in Cape Breton, indeed in all Canadian provinces, has been created by a Liberal administration which was in office for over 20 years.
Quite true.

speechtext: If something is now going wrong, particularly in Cape Breton, he might perhaps ask more questions and direct them to the Party he represents.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
1 was asked two questions in this long introduction. The first one was specifically related to Cape Breton.
Surely my colleague knows the special measures taken by the committees representing local interests, the provincial Government, which made their representations to the federal Government. They are now under review and should give some results.
When we talk about concerted efforts and co-operation with the provinces and local interests, it shows that we favour that kind of intervention, and local authorities make recommendations likely to meet the needs of the people.
As to what you refer to as losses, concerning equalization payments, I think it has been pointed out on several occasions that equalization payments had not been reduced, but there has been an indexation readjustment.
If you think the problem is peculiar to your province or to the Atlantic region, I can say it exists as well in Quebec, and that too may very well be due to the former administration which left us with a deficit which Canadians now want us to cut down.

You don't know anything.
