Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to take part in this debate today for more than one reason. One reason I am pleased is because it is a good and relevant motion and I thank my Liberal colleagues for having moved it today. The motion reads as follows:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of the people of Atlantic Canada in its demonstrated lack of political will to provide jobs and other economic opportunities to the people of that region.
I had the opportunity to visit Halifax, Wolfville and Sack-ville last week. That was not my first visit there but it was my most recent one. Actually, my great, great grandfather, Daniel McDonald, was a merchant in Halifax and I wanted to go


Supply
back to see how the city was doing. According to the people 1 met there and to the newspapers and other media that I saw, it is not doing quite as well as the rest of Canada.
There are three points to be raised today. I am especially concerned with housing and I was astonished to see the Hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) who is responsible for housing quoted as saying that there is no housing crisis in Halifax. What a frivolous statement he made. I will return to that point in a moment.
I was very pleased to see the local action that is being taken by people from those communities to create housing. They are not creating very much housing because their resources are limited but I was interested to see the action that they are taking and I will return to that in a moment.
As someone who is now living in and for two or three generations has belonged to what they call Upper Canada, I was embarrassed to see the financial fix in which Canada has put Nova Scotia. Of course, this is so not only for Nova Scotia but the other Atlantic provinces and I will return to that in a moment. The responsibility for that does not rest only with the previous Governments, it rests with the present one as well.
First, regarding the matter of the crisis, I visited Hope Cottage in downtown Halifax where Father McKenna explained that in 1982, 30,000 meals were given to homeless men; in 1984, 60,000, or double. If there are twice as many meals to be given to homeless men in 1984 as there were in 1982, how can we say that there is no crisis?
In fact, 35 responsible groups from Metropolitan Halifax including church groups, housing societies, health associations, welfare rights groups and the district labour council combined last summer to issue a report on the housing crisis. These are some of the things they mentioned: the cost of a three-bedroom apartment averages between $550 and $750 per month with many higher than that and single rooms cost $80 per week and up. Rents like that can be found in the City of Toronto but what cannot be found in Toronto is the large proportion of people whose incomes do not allow them to pay those prices. There are some but not in the proportion that exists in Halifax. It is pointed out that to afford that sort of accommodation, according to federal standards, a family's income should be between $26,000 and $36,000 per year.
They point out that federal funding for things like non-profit and co-op housing, which is the most reliable form of housing to provide for low income people and for middle income people, has been cut systematically during the last two years. It was cut by 25 per cent in the last year alone by this present Government. Only 252 new units have been constructed in the last five years in the Halifax district.
The crisis is not just a matter of buildings; it is a matter of what happens to the people who are either forced to live in poor buildings or forced to give up other necessities to live in a decent building. They catalogue the results, they summarize them: increased homelessness, families living in one or two rooms, family breakdown, physical and mental health deteriorating, unnecessary hospital admissions where the hospital keeps a child in hospital at great expense to the public because there is no heat or proper sanitary conditions in the home to which the child might be returned, food money getting spent on shelter and the frustration-frustration of the tenants, frustration of the homeowners in dismally poor homes, frustration of the workers, the human service workers, who are trying to hold the fabric of society together because they do not have the resources.
It has been demonstrated statistically over and over and it has been repeated in this House that the Atlantic provinces do not have the resources available to use for their own benefit. It is not that they have no natural resources. It is not that they have no good workers, willing and capable workers, but that they do not have the benefit of their natural resources and their labour resources. One measure of that is the figures from Statistics Canada which tell us that in Nova Scotia the income per capita is only 78.5 per cent of the average for all of Canada. Now, at that, they are better off than the other three Atlantic provinces. That is a long way down from average. The earned income per capita is only 74 per cent. Again, Nova Scotia is better off than New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, but it is only three-quarters of the average of Canada. Unemployment insurance payments per capita are 141 per cent of the national average, almost half as much again as is needed for the rest of the country. Again, the other provinces are in worse condition but Nova Scotia's condition is bad enough. The subsidies that are required per capita are 295 per cent of what is required in the other provinces. I will come back to that point again; but I want to mention the local drive, the local energy, in Wolfville.
I was shown what they call the small houses. These are houses locally designed. They are not CMHC houses; they are locally designed. There is one large room. They call them hearth houses, one large room where people cook, eat, and generally live and recreate and there are two small bedrooms, 600 square feet roughly. Now, by Toronto standards, that is a very, very small house. These are houses for people who are living outside Wolfville. They are living up in what they call the Mountain. They are replacing houses that were equally small but dreadfully, dreadfully poor houses with the wind blowing through, houses with one wood stove and a stove-pipe for a chimney set too close to the door. In wintertime there are not only tragedies of people who freeze for lack of fuel but people who burn because of the rickety stove in their house because they cannot afford better. Lack of decent water supply, lack of decent sewage arrangements. In these new small houses they have decent water supply. They have decent sewage arrangements. The houses are airtight, the heating equipment is modern and it has a brick chimney. The house is safe, comfortable and clean. It is of a design that many of the poeple there are used to. It is not only in Nova Scotia. When I lived in the Gatineau Valley for three years, 1 found that most of the farmhouses pratically worked with that design. They had a parlour but they never used it except when the minister came. He only used it once, found it too cold and then spent


with the rest of the family his time in the kitchen or diningroom. It is a good local effort and it did not cost the CMHC one cent. They neither used CMHC money, a CMHC guarantee nor a CMHC design. It was guaranteed by the local government.
In the city I saw Adsum House, a refuge for women. If you read the newspapers in Halifax you know it is badly needed, Mr. Speaker. I take my hat off to the people who keep that house going on a dreadfully small budget.
I saw co-ops, co-ops with 40 or 50 units that had been built in the last few years and one of them just being built, Seaview Co-op, again, with a great deal of local labour. In that case they had some help from CMHC but, as I say, that help has been declining.
The local people are trying to do what is needed. As I said before, they are in a condition in which it is not possible for them to get the full benefit of their local resources, whether it is natural or human. I want to demonstrate that in the case of one shocking example, the shell homes in Sackville. These are homes that were built a dozen or so years ago with CMHC initiation. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation built a shell and then conveyed it to a future homeowner on the understanding that the homeowner finish the shell inside and out, furnish it and so on. They are called shell homes. The roofs were so badly built that they are falling apart. They are rotting. They were built with moisture barriers above and below. There is no ventilation and they are rotting. I stood in the bedroom and looked at the plank that had been put in to hold up that part of the roof. The roof was sagging on each side of the plank. When I looked outside the roof looked like a ploughed field. This is one of 23 houses on that street, on that block. These were built under CMHC direction, that is, by Ottawa. They were inspected, so to speak, so we are told. Homeowners told me about seeing the day they came to take over the house and the inspector drove out, never walked close to the house, simply met the builder in his car out on the road and signed the final document of approval. He had never inspected the buildings then or before.
Shame!

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues are saying that it is shameful. I agree. I am particularly ashamed because the company that built those houses is a Toronto company, or was, before it went broke. There was a rip-off. Quite plainly there was a rip-off by that company building a substandard house and making whatever arrangements resulted in no inspection, getting clearance from CMHC for what it did and sticking the local homeowners with the garbage and, eventually, with the bills because now they are having to pay $10,000, $15,000, $18,000 to put on a new roof. One who was waiting for negotiations with CMHC waited too long and the roof fell in on her while she slept. She had to put a new roof on without any assistance from CMHC. Only three years ago one of these houses was resold. CMHC renewed its certificate of approval for that building which it knew was rotten. The officials of CMHC knew the building was rotten, mainly the roof, but not
Supply
only the roof. There were problems with the windows, the doors and the floors. If we take away the roof, the walls and floors, the house is all right but one cannot live in it. CMHC knew it was rotten yet it gave a certificate of approval to deceive a co-op into buying that unit from the former owner. Therefore there was a connivance between the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Toronto builder to cheat the people of Sackville. This concerns not only Sackville but houses in other provinces. We do not know where. CMHC knows, but it is not telling. We do not know how many shell homes were built and how many people were caught in that shell game which CMHC mastermined.
Those people are mostly poor. One of them said he had to double his mortgage to put on a roof. Another lady had applied for a RRAP grant but could not get it because she is too poor. Her husband has nothing but a disability pension. She could not repay the loan part so she is not entitled to receive the grant part. How she is going to put a new roof on her house, no one has told her. But the final crunch in this disgrace is that the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), responsible for housing and for the CMHC, is copping out. In March the local Member of the Legislature wrote to him about the problem. In April the Minister of Labour responsible for CMHC, thanked him for his letter and said that senior officials of Canada Mortgage and Housing had been requested to conduct an investigation into the problems outlined in the letter, including the aspect of CMHC responsibility for inspection of the houses. He said: "They will be contacting your office to obtain the names and addresses of home owners that are known to you". He also requested that the corporation examine mechanisms and programs such as may be available to provide assistance to the home owners. He said: "I expect to be able to provide you with the results of our investigations by early June". That was the Minister's signed promise. He never lived up to it. On June 18, Mr. Gordon Walt of CMHC in Ottawa telephoned the local MLA to tell him that a formal letter would be sent to him within the next two weeks in response because the inspections had been completed and it was agreed that the houses were in poor condition, particularly with design and maintenance problems. On August 8, the MLA, Johm Holme, wrote again to Mr. Gordon Walt. He said: "During our conversation of a few weeks ago, you indicated you would shortly be forwarding to me a copy of the interim report on the problem with shell housing in Sackville, Nova Scotia". He continues: "I've learned from Mr. Green in the Halifax CMHC office that he has not yet received the report but that the case has been referred to Vickie Garland of Social Housing for Block Funding". But still no report.
On August 15, Mr. Walt writes back to Mr. Holme. He says: "I have requested that Mr. McKnight's office reply directly to your August 8 letter which has been forwarded to him". On September 11 there is still no report. But Sylvain Lasnier, a special assistant to the Hon. Minister of Labour writes to Mr. Holme on behalf of the Minister: "I wish to


Supply
acknowledge receipt of your letter of August 8 concerning new houses built under the shell housing program. You can be assured that your correspondence would be brought to the Minister's attention at the earliest opportunity". I do not know where the Minister has been since August 28 but it would seem that he has not been in his office because he has not responded. On August 28, in fact, Mr. Holme wrote again to the Minister. He said: "It's my understanding from talking to Mr. Walt and other CMHC officials that the investigation and preliminary report were completed in early June". He asks for the report which the Minister-not an official-had promised him. On October 17, Mr. Holme writes again to the Minister: "Further to my correspondence of that date, I would like to inform you of a situation of which I've only recently become aware". He mentions a new development regarding that co-op house. He asks again for the report which the Minister had promised he would have in June.
Finally, there is again a letter from John Holme, MLA, on November 5 to the Minister: "In addition, I again ask that your Department provide me with a copy of their report prepared by your staff on the problems which exist with shell housing in Sackville". As of last Wednesday, no report had been received by John Holme. In other words, the Minister has decided it would be wiser not to issue the report he promised. He has offered a miserable $50,000 to put the roofs on 23 houses. That is $2,000 for a $10,000, $15,000 or $18,000 roof for poor people who were not responsible for its condition.
I am terribly sorry to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has elapsed.
Can I just finish briefly, Mr. Speaker?
Yes, you may.

What I wanted to say is that is the situation up to date at present. This Government, which the Progressive Conservative Party inherited and which enjoys spending the loot in all the ways Government spends the loot, has inherited the debt and obligation to put the roofs back on these houses in Sackville and in other parts of the Maritime Provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make some comments on the speech of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). Let me begin where he began, by pointing out that the motion before the House relates to economic opportunities for Atlantic Canada. I want to say two things. First, the Hon. Member has not addressed in any way, shape or form the serious matter of equal opportunities for Atlantic Canada. Instead, he related to us his trip in which he visited two of the wealthiest areas of the Atlantic Provinces, namely, the City of Halifax and the Town of Wolfville. He indicated the dire straits in which people found themselves in those urban centres. I want to say to this man who emerges from the heart of the City of Toronto that we in Nova Scotia do not think that the City of Halifax is in the dire straits which the Hon. Member apparently saw. In fact, those who traverse Yonge Street and the other parts of the City of Toronto, would probably welcome the opportunity to come to the City of Halifax and see the beauty and
splendour and magnificent development which has taken place there within the last eight years. Particularly since the advent of the John Buchanan Government in the Province of Nova Scotia, the city has actually blossomed. Hotels are constructed, freeways have been built. The city is in magnificent shape and is acclaimed by one and all to be one of the most magnificient cities in North America.
I would like the Hon. Member from the City of Toronto to stand up in this House of Commons and say that the City of Halifax does not compare in every way and in every detail with the City of Toronto or any other city in North America. I would like to ask him if his point was to discredit the area. The Town of Wolfville, the home of Acadia University, is one of the nicest towns in the whole of eastern Canada and does not deserve to be maligned in that way by the Hon. Member.
I simply want to ask the Hon. Member what does he know about Howland Drive in Sackville after a two hour journey up and down the street? What has he done? What has he written to the Minister responsible for housing? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what he and his colleagues in the New Democratic Party have done to the residents of Howland Drive, those unfortunate people who have a real problem which requires a real solution. They have made the case public. It is a kind of living off the avails of misfortune. It is the kind of thing the New Democratic Party has practised in this House and across this country since Adam was a boy. That is its point. It picks up destitute people, fans their case across the country and then tries to take credit for resolving it. The very fact they bring it to the public's attention in that way prevents a solution. What happens to a public servant when you accuse him of all kinds of wrongdoing like the Hon. Member for Spadina did in this Chamber and as his colleague, John Holmes, did in Nova Scotia in the media? The civil servant becomes defensive, refuses to co-operate. They take legal action, consult lawyers and say they cannot accept responsibility for this horrible situation. That is what happens. The matter becomes a stalemate and you cannot get a favourable answer from the official concerned. They deny any knowledge of it.
The case the Hon. Member mentions arose in 1972 and involved Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, as he said, it was a Toronto contractor who was the author of this terrible misfortune. He disappeared, probably into the confines of Spadina, and cannot be found. These other people are left with the problem. However, some of us are working diligently to provide a solution notwithstanding the posturing of people like John Holmes and the Hon. Member for Spadina. We want to resolve the problem, not live off the avails. Answer that.

Mr. Speaker, I would be glad to answer the Hon. Member on several points. He accuses me of hobnobbing with the well-to-do as well as meeting the poor. In fact, 1 met some of both. I made no comment on the general nature of Halifax. However, I did find that the Mayors and Wardmen, four of them, of Metroplitan Halifax agreed there is a housing crisis.


They agreed with the housing coalition. Of course the Hon. Member is then in a spot. He has to back his Minister who says there is no crisis. However, I said nothing about Halifax and Dartmouth and other cities which is not being said by people such as the mayor, the leading clergy, responsible academics, homeowners, tenants and the homeless in those cities.
As to exposing the facts about shell homes and shell games in Sackville, the Hon. Member has acknowledged this problem came to light in 1972.
Originated.

I heard from homeowners there about their efforts to try and get an answer from the Hon. Member, their MP, and how he turned them off and snubbed them. I understand why the Hon. Member is very defensive. He knows he has not done his job as their Member of Parliament. He knows his Minister has let them down and broken his promise to issue a report. He is thoroughly embarrassed by the fact his Government is just as irresonsible as the Government which preceded it.
Not as irresponsible as John Holmes.

The only way he can cover up is to make a thundering speech about someone who wants to get a legal defence and suggest that the rotten contractor, whose address is in Willowdale, must be hiding out in Spadina. Quite possibly he is. He went broke and we have a lot of poor people in Spadina. I am not afraid to admit we have poor people in Toronto. The point I was trying to make, and I am sorry the Hon. Member was so frantic that he would not get the point, is that money which should have been spent to fully benefit some people in Nova Scotia was instead partly drained away to Toronto not only by a shady contractor but by an irresponsible CMHC for which the present Minister has accepted full responsibility. Therefore, he cannot get out of paying his moral debts.

Mr. Speaker, I usually accept criticism gladly but I do not like to accept misrepresentation of the facts. 1 know that could not possibly be deliberate on the part of the Hon. Member so I will offer the further comment that we have been working diligently with the homeowners on Howland Drive to solve their problem.
That is not what they said.

What prevents solution of the problem is the fact that the officials of CMHC will not admit any of the facts which the Hon. Member presented to the House today. However, I will be very glad to take his allegations-he used the words "cheat" and "malice"-and present them to officials of CMHC. Perhaps, given what appear to be outlandish statements on the part of the Hon. Member for Spadina, officials of CMHC will be required to search their records and their consciences to determine whether or not they ought to acknowledge more responsibility. However, for the Member to
Supply
stand in this House and accuse any Member, and particularly the Government as a whole, of not recognizing their obligations when he well knows it is the officials of CMHC who deny any responsibility-
Where is the report that was promised eight months ago?

The Hon. Member well knows the status of CMHC. It is probably one of those many Crown corporations like Petro-Canada and CBC which are constantly defended by Members of the NDP. They constantly demand that these Crown corporations maintain their independent status and freedom from political intervention. That is why the Minister cannot call the shots. It is the officers in the corporations who are calling the shots and I object to that.

Mr. Speaker, the motion of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), moved earlier today, would see the House condemn the Government for abandoning the people of Atlantic Canada and for a lack of political will to provide jobs and economic opportunities. I believe the Hon. Member had his tongue in his cheek while speaking. If he did not, perhaps he should have, because I know that he knows that this Government has done an awful lot toward fostering economic development in the Atlantic region over the last 15 months. In fact, the Conservative Party is fully committed to development of the Atlantic region and my province in particular. I am very pleased that in just over one year we can point to a great deal of success in the development of Prince Edward Island and the Atlantic region.
One of the first items of priority for our Government in Atlantic Canada, and P.E.I. in particular, was to overlook the formula of the Hon. Member's Government concerning equalization payments to the poorer provinces. Despite the fact that Liberal legislation would have seen us in a very serious situation because of declining equalization payments, our Government overlooked the formula and added money to the pot. We recognized that the Atlantic provinces needed the financial assistance, which should have been there anyway, to ensure they continue with full economic development. Prince Edward Island alone received some $2 million we would not have otherwise received only through the good graces of the Conservative Government on this side of the House.
There were many other issues addressed in the last year. To start off with the fishery, I was very pleased that the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans moved quickly to resolve a long-standing problem which had not been addressed by the former Liberal Government. We were denied crab licences for years and years despite successive requests to Liberal Ministers of the day. Can you imagine a province in the middle of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, completely surrounded by water, with a crab resource off its shores and the Government said no, we could not have access to that fishery? The Conservative Minister quickly redressed that problem last fall. He gave us 16 exploratory permits and that led to landings of approximately one million pounds of snow-crab. That translates into a lot of economic returns for my province. It meant jobs for


Supply
fishermen, their helpers on the boats and plant workers on shore. Those plant workers were not just in P.E.I., they were in neighbouring provinces such as New Brunswick. Based on the success in year one I think we will see this Government continue to aid that fishery in our province because the resource is there. I know that that is not a major cost to government, but it is simply a matter of doing justice to the provinces.
Today opposition Members bewailed reductions in transportation services. I would like to speak for a few minutes about some of the things that have happened in my own constituency which indicate that transportation services and facilities have not all been reduced as has been suggested by Hon. Members. For example, after the election last fall the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) moved quickly to ensure that we had additional ferry crossings from Wood Island, P.E.I., to Caribou, Nova Scotia. At that time there was a crisis in terms of getting agricultural products, highway material, and many items required by industry generally, from Nova Scotia to P.E.I. The additional crossings were allowed at considerable expense to the federal treasury.
That was not all, Mr. Speaker. During the winter months negotiations continued between the Department and Northumberland Ferries Limited, the carrier, and as a result we had better service last summer. There were additional crossings between P.E.I. and Nova Scotia which produced direct economic benefit to my constituency as well as the entire province. When the ferries are not running or are making less crossings, we feel the impact immediately. When the ferry runs open up, our economy opens up. Tours can go in and out and people can access markets more easily. The Government has shown leadership in that area.
Not only has the Government improved service, but it has entered into negotiations with Northumberland Ferries for the construction of new vessels for that run. Currently negotiations are under way which could result in two 150-car ferries installed for the run between Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. That would be a tremendous economic benefit to my province.
Another transportation matter which is important to the constituency of Cardigan is that the Government, through the Minister of Transport, approved a $5.4 million contract for the reconstruction of the Georgetown wharf which was burned a few years ago. That wharf is very important to the eastern end of the province. Georgetown is a deep-water harbour used to load potato boats and pulp boats. It is also used by the Georgetown shipyard for repairing vessels which dock at the wharf. The port is used to unload asphalt, oil, and gas for a local oil company. That initiative, which was delayed, postponed, and pushed around with a long stick by the former Government, was acted upon quickly by the Minister of Transport. He has come up with funding for that very important project. In addition, he has approved the expenditure of $2 million in the town of Surrey for expansion of its wharf
facilities. That is another benefit to the transportation industry and the fishing sector.
The Government has also assisted the agricultural industry. The hog industry in Prince Edward Island has been in crisis due to the fact that our main processing plant, a Canada Packers operation, was due to be closed by the owners. The plant was an antique, unable to keep up to standards and inspections which was losing money year after year. The provincial Conservative Government moved quickly after the decision by Canada Packers to ensure that the plant did not close and that our hog industry would not suffer serious consequences. It moved quickly in concert with producers of hogs and beef cattle, but it could not get the co-operation of the former Liberal Government.
I am pleased to say that once the federal Government was elected serious negotiations began between the province, the producers, and the federal Government. Those negotiations resulted in $4.5 million of federal money being spent for the construction of a new plant which is now nearing completion. That plant will be paid for by hog producers, beef producers, and the province. The plant will actually be operated by Canada Packers under an agreement to manage and market the product from that plant. That has enabled us to consider expanding our hog industry and, more important, it has enabled us to save the existing industry.
I would like to mention a few more economic initiatives so that people will not get the idea that only a few things have happened. In the last 15 months $6.8 million has been made available to P.E.I. for industrial competitiveness programs. There has been an expenditure of $3.2 million for IRDP offers. A commitment in the amount of $10 million has been made to the Atlantic Veterinary College in Charlottetown. There has been an allocation of $7.3 million for a new terminal building at the Charlottetown airport. There has been an allocation of $1.8 million for the dredging of the Summerside harbour so that it can receive potato boats necessary to export our process. There has been an expenditure of $.35 million to establish the Eastern Ventures and Development Corporation in my constituency which is now providing funds to enable small businesses to start up. There has been a provision of $8 million to CFB Summerside in order to establish a mess and hospital facility. Federal money amounting to $5.8 million has been allocated under a new tourism agreement which will allow us to continue to build on the tourism base which already exists in the province. Five million dollars has been spent on marketing and $5.2 million has been spent on industrial milk assistance. There has been a $7.5 million expenditure on fisheries and a $13.6 million on forestry.
That is all federal money committed by the Conservative Government to ensure that jobs are created in P.E.I. It is just one more indication of the fact that we have not, in any way, shape, or form, abandoned economic priorities in Atlantic Canada.
I have not mentioned the big item yet, Mr. Speaker. The Conservative Government acted on a commitment made by our Leader prior to the election to address the very serious


problem of electrical energy costs in our province. P.E.I. has been plagued for years by the highest electrical rates anywhere in Canada. The Liberal Government refused to help the province to address that problem. 1 sometimes think that was because it did not want the provincial Conservative Government to get any credit for being able to get such an agreement. Although I hate to say it, Mr. Speaker, I think that economic development was being sacrificed for political credit. I hope that this Government never stoops to such a low.
This fall an historic agreement was signed. It will create jobs because lower electrical energy costs mean that our industries can be competitive. Some $50 million has been allocated to the federal-provincial agreement. That will offer up to 40 per cent assistance to manufacturers and processors who will be able to increase their industrial competitiveness. Over all, consumers of electrical energy will benefit by approximately 20 per cent.
Job creation has been talked about by Members opposite all day. They have suggested that jobs are not being created in Atlantic Canada and that the Government has abandoned its commitment for the creation of jobs. Once again, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, the Government has moved away from the old band-aid approach of job creation. Job creation funds have been restructured so that we will no longer have make-work projects and dead-end jobs but will be able to assist people who want to be trained for permanent jobs in the private sector and want to assist in the growth and development of our economy. We have committed equal dollars to the training and development of unemployed Atlantic Canadians.
Last summer, Challenge 85 was introduced. That was an important variation of the old summer job-creation projects. For the first time substantial money was made available to the private sector to employ people. Some of that money has led to more permanent work. It has provided students with training in the private sector which will give them opportunities in the future. That is a substantial departure from the old job creation projects which were simply government projects that led nowhere and had no lasting benefit.
1 just mention the new Canadian Jobs Strategy as well. An agreement was signed between the federal and provincial Governments for an approach to economic development and job creation in the Atlantic area. That was unheard of under the former Liberal Government. Some 1,000 projects have already been approved in the Maritimes. Contrary to opposition statements, it is clear that we have not abandoned job creation in Atlantic Canada. One only need look at the Statistics Canada figures for proof. In July this year, Prince Edward Island had the largest labour force ever. There were some 64,000 people in our labour force. That does not suggest a migration from the province as suggested by the opposition earlier or abandonment of the province. It shows more health in our economy than ever before.
Supply
Even though there was high unemployment in November, which we do not want to endure, it is important that we look at all of the statistics. There were 57,000 people in the labour force which is up by 3,000 over 1984. Employment was also up by 1,000 people over November, 1984. Our participation rate was up by 1.7 per cent. These figures which are similar for the last 12 months show that more people are working. The labour force is increasing, there is greater involvement in our economy and more economic activity is taken place. Our Government has had a good record, especially in its first year, after so many years of Liberal neglect of Atlantic Canada.
I am not pretending that problems do not exist in my province or the Atlantic area. I will not begin burying my head in the sand and suggesting that all is well and good. We intend to address those problems just as we did with respect to those items I mentioned earlier.
There is no question that we have problems with agriculture. Today, some 24 tobacco farmers from my constituency of Cardigan were present on Parliament Hill and in the House. They were here because they are concerned about the tobacco industry in Canada, particularly in Prince Edward Island. They are considering the advantages of establishing a national marketing agency.
I believe it is important that I point out that the Government acted early to amend the National Farm Products Marketing Act to enable tobacco to be included among the commodities where a national marketing agency could be established. That development has been held up by a court injunction. However, I believe that justice will prevail and the growers will be able to make the right decision in regard to the tobacco industry in the months ahead. I look forward to closely working with them.
The other day I rose under the provisions of Standing Order 22 to speak to the House about the pending financial disaster facing our tobacco producers. I suggested to the Government that growers will have to be compensated for loss of productive capacity. I will continue to press the Government on this important issue.
Similarly, our potato growers are experiencing serious difficulties, with three years of prices well below the cost of production. In fact, it cost roughly 6 cents to produce a pound of potatoes but our growers are only getting 2 cents to 2.5 cents for their commodity. It would not take very long for even the strongest producers to run far into the red and border on the verge of bankruptcy. Indeed, some have already gone bankrupt.
The federal and provincial governments, along with the growers, must work diligently to ensure that the potato industry in my province does not collapse. The potato industry is the backbone of the Prince Edward Island agricultural industry. When one thinks of Prince Edward Island, one thinks of potatoes and lobsters. Thank goodness that lobsters are strong this year because potatoes have not been strong for three years. It is a serious situation and I intend to work side by side


Supply
with the growers in the potato industry to ensure that they get the kind of assistance that is necessary.
Even today, representatives of the P.E.I. potato industry met with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). Once again, the Government is showing its concern for the province. I believe that it will act by providing appropriate assistance in the very near future. The opposition is wrong. The Government has not abandoned Atlantic Canada but has perhaps done more in one year than the last 10 years of Liberal administration.
If the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond reflected on his motion for a moment, he would probably withdraw it, realizing that he has made a serious error. If he will not withdraw it, perhaps he will amend his motion to condemn the former Government rather than the present Government for abandoning Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the second time today that the Member for Cardigan (Mr. Binns), in searching desperately to find an example of positive programs that have been undertaken by the current administration, has had to reach back to the days of the Liberal administration. In the case of Newfoundland he read a list of six projects, all of which were undertaken by the previous Government.
In the case of Prince Edward Island, he talked about the veterinarian college, the Charlottetown airport, the move of Veterans Affairs, the dredging of Summerside Harbour and about CFB Summerside. All of these projects were initiated under the able representation of my colleague, and seat-mate, the Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson).
Members opposite could learn a lesson from him. As a Member of the Government and a Government supporter, he was never one to sit by silently when policies were being contemplated that were not in the best interest of his constituents. It might come as a shock to back-benchers opposite, particularly Members from Atlantic Canada from whom we have not heard, that Members of Parliament such as the Member for Egmont understood that while his loyalty and responsibility was to the development of the nation, he must speak with a particular voice for the people of his riding. He did so even when he found himself in conflict with the Government of the day. That is why we have such a list of progressive and positive projects which have contributed significantly to the Province of Prince Edward Island. I should say, with a degree of modesty, that the same is true in the Province of Newfoundland.
The motion today reads:
That this House condemns the Government for its abandonment of the people of Atlantic Canada in its demonstrated lack of political will to provide jobs and other economic opportunities to the people of that region.
Ever since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) delivered his economic statement, or mini-Budget, to the House in November, 1984, the policy in this country has been to move toward the notion of user pay. This is a notion which for the first time in decades espouses the belief that we are no longer willing to pay a price to ensure that all Canadians, no matter
where they live, no mater what their economic circumstances, shall have certain basic rights and services afforded to them by the national Government. The policy being enunciated by the Progressive Conservative Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), follows a philosophy that the price of providing basic equality for Canadians wherever they live in this country has suddenly become too high.
We have a Government that is going to cut by way of transfer payments not luxury items, not four-lane highways, not tourism development dollars but education and health care. We are saying to the people who live in the poorest provinces of Canada that they no longer should expect to move in those two fundamental primary areas toward a sense of equality with people who live in the wealthier parts of this country, quite the opposite. "You should expect if you live in an area of disparity, of high unemployment, an area with a relatively low degree of wealth, that services will degenerate, regress. People should check with their fathers and grandfathers, their mothers and grandmothers and find out what it was like 30 years ago because we are taking you back with this policy of the Government."
In 1976 a Member of Parliament stood in this House and talked about his concern that the commitment of the Liberal Government of the day toward regional development was being diminished. He said:
It is beyond my comprehension how any Government can restrain expenditures in an area of the country which has an unemployment rate of 13.9 per cent. It is, in fact, positively cruel and inhuman for any Government to apply a restraint policy equally across this country as though every section of it is the same. It may be a policy of restraint that is quite apt for provinces like Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan, perhaps where are now high employment figures but is not proper to apply it blindly to Newfoundland which has an unemployment rate of almost 14 per cent.
Those words were spoken in 1976 by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the former Minister of Finance, now the Minister of Justice. He was talking about Newfoundland with an unemployment rate of 14 per cent and saying that the province could not afford a policy of restraint.
That 14 per cent unemployment has now become 20 per cent. The roar of the Member for St. John's West in opposition to Government restraint and cut-backs at 14 per cent in 1976 has now become a whimper, a pathetic whimper of approval for restraint and cut-backs at a time when my province is experiencing, nine years later, unemployment of 20 per cent, and unemployment on the increase in the last 14 months since this Government has taken office.
What does the Government do? It wields a surgical scalpel. It cuts. It has gone through the fat and the meat. It is into the bone, and still it cuts deep into the marrow, Mr. Speaker. What do we mean? In Newfoundland we talk about marrow. Do we mean that the people in Newfoundland can no longer afford to have two cars? Is that what we mean? No, Mr. Speaker. It is not what we mean. That is not marrow. That is fat. Do we mean that the people of Newfoundland can no longer afford to buy three Canada Savings Bonds so will only


buy one? They cannot afford any right now, but that is not marrow either. That is also fat. The fat of the land is something we only dream about these days in the Province of Newfoundland.
When I say that this Government's economic scalpel has cut right to the bone marrow in the Province of Newfoundland, what I mean is that Newfoundlanders are beginning to lose hope. They are being swept up in a tide of cynicism, anger, frustration and hopelessness. Yes, Mr. Speaker, they are becoming convinced that they are the human disposables in a society being crafted by a Government that bows down before the altar of market forces, in a world that must conform to the theology of user pay and to a throw away society. There is nothing so tragic as a people without hope.
There can be no greater waste anywhere in our society than in a young mind afflicted with the curse of cynicism. There are too many tragic people in my province. There are too many good young minds that have been poisoned by the frustration and anger that comes with cynicism.
You know the cynic, Mr. Speaker. Every Member in this Elouse recognizes a cynic when he sees one. He is the young man or young woman who does not trust anybody, the person who believes that nothing he or she can do will change anything, the person who believes that everyone is out for himself or herself. The cynic is seduced by the option of copping out, seduced by the option of sitting on the sidelines and condemning all of those who would attempt to chart their own course and who attempts to fasten the fabric of society in which they live.
The message of the Government is to cut, cut and cut some more. If you are patient enough, if you bow down before the altar of market forces and believe in the philosophy of user pay, one day down the road, somewhere, God knows when, it will all be all right, you simply have to have faith.
As this Government begs for faith, the ranks of the cynics are swelling and we are losing the most important resource this country possesses, the good young minds, the heart and soul of the country, which is eating itself in frustration and anger in a sense of hopelessness.
I say to the Government, as has been said to the Government by the Conservative, same stripe Premier of Nova Scotia, by the Conservative same stripe Premier of Newfoundland, by the Conservative same stripe Premier of Prince Edward Island, by the Conservative same stripe Premier of New Brunswick, by opposition leaders in all four of those provinces and by the Atlantic Provinces Chambers of Commerce, the Transportation Commission, and Economic Council, indeed the voice of the people of Atlantic Canada, that this policy is not going to work.
The people of Atlantic Canada unquestionably would prefer to live in a society where they would not need to have a hand-out, and would unquestionably prefer to be giving, contributing to the pot that sits at the centre of the country, not depending upon the wealth of those elsewhere. Until that day arrives, until we find in a very complex and difficult world, a
Supply
changing world, the kind of solution that allows us to make the contribution we want to make to the nation as a whole, do not in the name of some ideological political philosophical doctrin-naire position about the market-place take away from Atlantic Canada the underpinning of our economy, socially and economically. Do not say to our young people, those who just want a chance to have the dignity of a job and the dignity of a paycheque, that they are part of a disposable society. That is the greater tragedy being inflicted upon Atlantic Canada with the economic measures of this administration.
I give way in the hope that my colleague the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) will be able to add his voice to this debate.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, on the last point made by the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) I will speak for only 10 minutes and allow the remainder of the time to go to one of our colleagues.
I rise in this debate not as someone new speaking on opposition days with concern about Atlantic Canada because when the previous Liberal Government was in power our caucus was making exactly the same kind of resolution in the House. Many of the items I will speak about relating to Government neglect, taxation policies and the way the Government's actions have impacted on the people of Atlantic Canada are the same types of things that I was saying four years ago in a similar debate.
The problems in Atlantic Canada are not new. Historically they have not been caused by any one Government. However, the people of that region are legitimately concerned about them. Their concerns have been expressed in the House over a number of years. The people of the region have every reason to expect that the Government will not neglect or continue to neglect their problems. They have every reason to expect that we, as a Parliament, will actually deal with some of the proposals.
It is with that in mind that I wrote to the chairperson of the Standing Committee on Regional Development. I asked for that committee to travel to Atlantic Canada to take a look at what was happening. I indicated that we could use another in-depth study of the area. I suggested that if the committee did not have the time to tour all Atlantic Canada, it could use the very tragic situation of Cape Breton as a study model. I hope Hon. Members of all three Parties support that committee spending time to consider the situation and to make an extensive tour of the Cape Breton area. Other colleagues in my caucus have written to the same committee asking for an in-depth study, so that the people of the region could make presentations. I hope the committee will take the opportunity to visit there and to conduct a very intensive study.
I have visited Atlantic Canada a number of times in the last three months. For that matter, I have made three trips in the


Supply
last 75 days, for the sole purpose of hearing what the people had to say about the Government and what was happening to them. I visited Cape Breton as well as the mainland of Nova Scotia. There are many concerns, some of which resulted from the May 23 Budget. For example, the workers at the heavy water plants were laid off and only heard that fact as they listened to the budget speech on television. They were certainly affected by the actions of the Government. Two weeks prior to the presentation of the Budget, they were told by a Minister of the Crown that before anything happened to the heavy water plants they would be consulted. Also they were told that other job programs would be in place before anything happened to them.
Let us look at what happened. That is not what the Government in fact did. The more than 600 people working in those two heavy water plants turned on their television sets on budget night and heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), with that one line in his Budget, tell them that their jobs had disappeared. It was a shameful action. It was a cruel and harsh measure. Even if the Government believed that it had to take that step, it could have been more concerned about how it dealt with the people affected. They should not have been required to turn on their television sets that night to hear from the Minister of Finance, without any explanation or expression or concern, that their jobs and, in many cases, their homes in those communities had disappeared. That harshness or cruelty is typified in many of the decisions made by the Government.
Shame.

It is not only the present Government. As I said in my introductory remarks, it has not been only the Conservative Government. The Liberals cannot pretend, despite the mutterings of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), that these problems are new ones.
I should like to return to some of the concerns which I heard expressed in Atlantic Canada. I wrote to various Ministers about these concerns. For example, I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) about Sydney Steel Corporation and CN orders going to European manufacturers. That was not something new. The problems with Sydney Steel have existed for years. When the Liberals were in Government, we asked questions about Sydney Steel. We asked where was the money for phase two and when real action would take place on their commitment to those people. We are still awaiting that action. We were promised by the previous Liberal Government-and now the Conservative Government is promising it-that there would be money for phase two, yet the people of Sydney are still waiting. They were told that the decision would be made soon. They were told that in September and in October. They were told that a decision would be made before the end of October, and later they were told that it would be by the end of November. However, that decision has not come about. The previous Liberal administration and the present Conservative administration have talked a lot about Sydney Steel but have refused to act.
I have also written to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) about the workers in the heavy water plants in Cape Breton who were laid off. Many of the problems faced by those people were not only as a result of new Conservative measures respecting unemployment insurance. They also exist because there were cut-backs in the unemployment insurance program by the previous Liberal Government, and the Conservative Government continued along the same path.
I have written to many Ministers. For example, I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay). 1 wrote to the Minister of Transport about CN Marine and staff reductions in North Sydney. I have written to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and to the Minister of Finance. I have written many letters, such as the one to the Minister of National Revenue about the heavy water plant workers. I have been trying to point out that these people are facing serious problems. They are not new problems. No one can pretend that they came about on September 4, 1984 with the election of the Conservative Government. These are problems on which the Conservatives are now making very harsh decisions, very harsh on the people who live in those communities and work in those operations. They are a continuation of the years of neglect, the years of failing to come to grips with regional economic expansion. We must remember that the Liberals were in power for most of that period of time.
One of the most harsh decisions in so far as Atlantic Canada was concerned was when the previous Liberal decided to dismantle the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. That Department was incorporated within the new Department, at which time I rose, as well as others, and explained that in the long run less money would be going into the hinterland areas such as Atlantic Canada and more money would be going into large industries in the heartland. This means that as the country continues to grow, the hinterland areas will continue to be ignored. That is what has happened.
I attended as an observer at the First Ministers' Conference, and Conservative Premiers from Atlantic Canada said that we were suffering because the money for regional development was not keeping pace with other government expenditures. That was said by Conservative Premiers. They told that to the Conservative Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and other Ministers such as the Minister of Employment and Immigration. They said that the money was not forthcoming in the same proportion as it used to be. This results from the fact that there is no Department of Regional Economic Expansion with a specific mandate to ensure that the interests and concerns of the people living in those regions are looked after.
Again this is not strictly as a result of the neglect shown by the Conservatives. It is also a result of a decision made by the Liberal Government and a trend started by that Government to reduce the total amount of government expenditures directed toward regional economic expansion.
Before I sit down, and I made a promise to a Liberal Member that I would give him an opportunity to speak before


the debate ended, there is another item regarding Atlantic Canada about which I should like to speak. It is one of the reasons I went to the First Ministers' Conference and that is the Government's announcement in the Budget that it would be reducing expenditures for transfer payments by $2 billion annually. Transfer payments provide the money that goes to post-secondary education and medicare.
It does not matter to me that the Government is pretending that this is not a cut. I know that when they were in Opposition, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) were two of the chief critics of the Liberal Government when it did the same thing. Those two Ministers sat right here on the front benches and called the MacEachen Budget a cut that was breaking faith with the provinces. That is what they said then. Each of those Ministers said something to the effect that that would result in the closing of schools and the loss of beds for hospitals. I find it quite interesting that the Ministers who are actually responsible for health care and for providing money for medicare and post-secondary education are saying exactly the opposite now that they sit on the Government benches.
It is apparent, particularly in the area of medicare, that because of our growing population and because of the growing technology in the health field there are going to be cost increases in the field of health care, cost increases which will be much higher than the increase in the cost of living. For the Prime Minister to address the premiers and the House of Commons by saying that the Government will cover the cost of living and therefore the provinces should be grateful is for him to try to sell a myth. In fact, we know that the cost to the provinces for medicare and post-secondary education will increase by more than the cost of living.
For the Minister of Finance to say: "It's all right, boys and girls, it doesn't matter because we are going to cover at least the cost of living," ignores the fact that he is transferring the burden from the federal tax base to that of the provinces. The provinces will have to make up that shortfall. There is no region in Canada that will suffer more from that than Atlantic Canada. That is something with which the Government will have to come to grips. The Government broke a promise to the people of Atlantic Canada and that is something which will be remembered.
I recognize that there is not much time left in this debate and 1 will sit down soon, but in closing, I do want to say that the Government broke faith in so many areas that there really does now exist the cynicism about which the Liberal Member who spoke previously spoke so eloquently. However, Liberal Members must share much of the blame for that. They have to share that blame with the Conservative Members. What the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Health and Welfare and saying is exactly the opposite of what they said when they were in Opposition and that breeds cynicism. It certainly breeds cynicism in the area of this country which needs the most assistance in order to develop in its own way.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by thanking my hon. friend from Churchill (Mr. Murphy) for leaving me some of his time, and 1 would like to take advantage of the few minutes I have left to take stock of the situation. I would have liked to do so in greater detail, but I will do what I can in the circumstances. Mr. Speaker, if I were to paint a picture of everything the Conservative Government should do for Atlantic Canada, I think it would not be a very happy one, with very few bright spots.
Not a day goes by in Atlantic Canada without people asking me, when I am there: Why are we being ignored? Why have people forgotten we exist? Mr. Speaker, it is not just me-it is also what the people down there think. Not long ago, according to the results of a public opinion poll, the popularity rating of the Conservatives in this region dropped to 33 per cent. The Liberals went up to 43 per cent. And no wonder. It is because this Government has done nothing except implement negative development policies in our region. Especially if we consider the question of regional economic development and what has been done for the Atlantic provinces. The Budget was cut by S450 million. In the Atlantic provinces, the conclusion is that the Government is ignoring us and has forgotten that we exist. Mr. Speaker, the Government wants to let the market forces act, and we all know what happens when you do that. The large urban centres are the winners, and disadvantaged regions like ours are the losers.
Mr. Speaker, this Government has no regional development policy for the very simple reason that to have such a policy, one must first have the political will to help these regions. And that is exactly what this Government lacks.
Another example to explain why people in Atlantic Canada have lost confidence in the Government, is what is going to happen to transfer payments. We are told that these payments will not be reduced. No indeed! They will not be reduced, but just the same, it is going to cost New Brunswick about $120 million. And they say: Don't worry, it's peanuts.
I continue, Mr. Speaker. 1 am talking about fisheries which happen to be a labour-intensive sector in Atlantic Canada, yet the only thing they managed to do was to cut the budget for small craft harbours, and then they decided to ask the fishermen to pay for certain projects such as dredging and wharf repairs. It is totally ludicrous to expect low income fishermen to finance projects which are the responsibility of the Government. Even more so when we consider the program to help fishermen build their own boats-there is no money left!
Our fishing fleet will gradually become obsolete and there will be no money to replace it.

Let me say a few words about the CN shops in which 225 jobs have been lost. The Minister cannot today explain why this is so and he does not want to take any position which will guarantee to the people of Moncton that those jobs will be protected.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude by quoting a passage of La Sagouine which adequately describes the actions of this Government:
Sure enough, they say that promises will be made right, left and centre during the election campaign ... You will get everything for nothing because you are first class citizens with the right to vote ... It does not change anything, once the election is over the Government is too busy and could not care less about us.
